PART 1 [7 points]. Written comprehension. Choose one of the two options below and follow
the instructions to answer the questions.
Option 1.
                                            Greenwashing
 1     Being green is big business, with one study showing that 66% of consumers worldwide are
       willing to pay more for products they believe to be socially and environmentally responsible.
       However, shoppers should exercise caution when shopping sustainably, as much of the
       language companies use to sell their products is not what it seems. The practice of
       greenwashing involves companies making misleading or exaggerated environmental
       statements about their products in order to gain a competitive advantage over similar items
       on supermarket shelves. "Companies are under a lot of pressure to become eco-friendly
       because consumers are looking for this," explains eco-influencer Mandy Spooner, "so they
       present a 'greener' image of themselves through advertising and packaging."
 2     Some of the marketing tricks companies use include natural-looking imagery and vague
       terminology. For example, terms like biodegradable and compostable are often more
       complicated than they appear, as many products cannot be processed in a household
       compost bin and instead need specific commercial conditions to break down. Another strong
       example of a commonly greenwashed product is bottled water. Despite being marketed as
       clean and pure, the water industry drains local natural resources and uses vast quantities of
       petrol, shipping their "product" thousands of kilometres around the world. It is also a
       significant contributor to plastic waste. Just because a plastic water bottle is recyclable does
       not mean it will be.
 3     A significant fallout of greenwashing is that it can erode consumer confidence, as Spooner
       explains: "When companies make sustainability claims that turn out to be false, they not only
       damage their own reputation but also brands genuinely committed to doing the right thing."

         Greenwashing can have serious consequences. To tackle this issue, the UK government
         recently published the Green Claims Code, a set of guidelines to help companies comply
         with the law and clearly communicate their environmental credentials.
 4       So, how can consumers ensure they are buying truly sustainable products? A simple rule
         Spooner recommends is to always check the labels on the packaging and contact brands if
         their sustainability claims are vague or hard to understand: "It only takes a couple of minutes
         to email a company with a question or two." Spooner believes consumers have an obligation
         to ensure the products they buy are ethical and sustainable, as "the choices we make today
         can have a profound impact on the future." She explains, "Being a mum absolutely informs
         my decisions. I try to live sustainably for my children and for generations to come.”
                                                           Adapted from Yahoo! News, December 2025

PART 1 [7 points]. Written comprehension. Choose one of the two options below and follow the
instructions to answer the questions.

Option 1.
                                         Screen time in Japan
 1 Amid growing concerns about excessive screen time, the city council of Toyoake in Japan is
   asking its residents to limit their recreational use of smartphones and tablets to no more than
   two hours per day. Official guidelines on the use of digital devices came into municipal law in
   October 2025. The mayor of Toyoake explained: “Digital technologies are wonderful, but it is
   important to limit the time we spend on them for non-work or non-educational purposes. We
   also need to think about our youth. Many children and teenagers have their own smartphones
   and bedrooms. With nothing else to do, they spend hours staring at screens. Day turns to
   night, their sleep suffers, and the cycle repeats.” The primary purpose of the law is to ensure
   sufficient sleeping hours among children and adolescents. For children aged 6 to 12, the
   guidelines recommend switching off phones and tablets by 9:00 pm to ensure that sleep is
   not disturbed. Older children, and even adults, are encouraged to switch off by 10:00 pm.
 2 The Toyoake city council first proposed the law in August and immediately received criticism
   from residents. Local councillor Mariko Fujie argued: “Many residents believe this is total
   nonsense. For my part, I feel a strong resistance to regulating people's free time with a law.”
   Councillor Fujie also published an open letter in the local newspaper arguing that the
   guidelines were not based on scientific evidence. However, several studies carried out in Asia
   have confirmed the negative impact of screen time on wellbeing. For example, one study of
   teenagers in China found that sleep patterns, social relationships, and academic performance
   were all negatively affected by the number of hours participants spent on their devices.

 Inglés                                                                                              2 de 6



 3 In reality, the law is more symbolic than enforced. The Toyoake city council will not track
   residents’ phone usage, and it will not issue fines to those who exceed the recommended
   two-hour limit. Instead, the guidelines are more about encouraging users to carefully consider
   their screen time. Although the measure was controversial at first, many residents have
   responded positively to it. University student Shoki Moriyama has reduced his screen time
   from eight hours to just under two, admitting that although it had been a struggle, it was worth
   it: “I now use that extra time to study or go to the gym.” Local resident Akari Saito agrees: “I
   found it especially hard to put my phone away during the train to school or while I was walking,
   but I can see that reducing my phone use will allow me to spend my day more meaningfully.”
                                                              Adapted from Time, December 2025
